slides.narration: Every power station, every transformer on an electric pole and every induction cooktop runs on one discovery: a changing magnetic field can drive a current. In this part we define magnetic flux, state Faraday’s laws, find the direction of the induced current with Lenz’s law, work out the emf across a moving rod, and see the currents that swirl inside solid metal.

slides.heading: Magnetic flux
slides.body_md:
For a flat coil of area $A$ in a uniform field $B$, the **magnetic flux** through it is
$$\Phi = \vec B \cdot \vec A = BA\cos\theta$$
where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec B$ and the **normal** to the coil. Unit: **weber** (1 Wb = 1 T m²). For $N$ turns the **flux linkage** is $N\Phi$.
bullets: Largest (BA) when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to B; zero when the plane is parallel to B.
Careful: an angle given between the field and the PLANE of the coil must be changed to 90° minus that angle.

slides.narration: Magnetic flux measures how much field passes through a surface. For a flat coil it is the field times the area times the cosine of the angle between the field and the normal to the coil. The unit is the weber, one tesla square metre. Watch the angle: in the diagram the plane of the coil is at thirty degrees to the field, so the normal is at sixty degrees, and the flux is half of B A.

slides.heading: Faraday’s laws of electromagnetic induction
slides.body_md:
**First law:** whenever the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an emf is induced in it; it lasts only while the change continues.
**Second law:** the induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage:
$$\varepsilon = -N\,\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$$
bullets: The flux can change through B, through A or through the angle θ.
The minus sign is Lenz’s law (next slides). Induced current $I = \varepsilon/R$.

rows: Magnet held still inside the coil
Current switched on in a nearby coil

visual.alt: Table of Faraday’s observations: a galvanometer connected to a coil deflects only while the flux through the coil is changing, more for a faster change, and in opposite directions for opposite changes

slides.narration: Faraday found that a galvanometer joined to a coil deflects only while something changes: a magnet moving in or out, or a current switched on in a nearby coil. Hold the magnet still and the needle returns to zero. Move it faster and the kick is bigger. His second law makes this exact: the emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage, N times d phi by d t, with a minus sign we will meet soon.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: emf, current and charge
slides.body_md: A coil of 50 turns, each of area 80 cm², lies with its plane perpendicular to a field that rises steadily from 0.10 T to 0.50 T in 0.080 s. The circuit resistance is 5.0 Ω. Find the emf, the current and the charge that flows.
bullets: Step 1 — change of flux per turn: $\Delta\Phi = \Delta B\,A = 0.40 \times 80 \times 10^{-4} = 3.2 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb.
Step 2 — $\varepsilon = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{50 \times 3.2 \times 10^{-3}}{0.080} = 2.0$ V; $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R} = 0.40$ A.
Step 3 — $q = I\Delta t = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R} = \dfrac{50 \times 3.2 \times 10^{-3}}{5.0} = 0.032$ C, the same however fast the change.

visual.alt: Worked table: flux change 3.2 milliwebers per turn, emf 2 volts, current 0.4 amperes, charge 0.032 coulombs

slides.narration: Each turn gains three point two milliwebers of flux. Fifty turns, in eight hundredths of a second, give an emf of two volts, and with five ohms the current is point four amperes. The charge is the current times the time, point zero three two coulombs. Notice that it equals N times the flux change over R: the time cancels, so a slow change moves the same charge as a quick one.

slides.heading: Reading a flux–time graph
slides.body_md: The emf per turn is the **slope** of the $\Phi$–$t$ graph (with a minus sign):
bullets: 0 to 1.5 s: slope 2.0 mWb s⁻¹, so 2.0 mV per turn.
1.5 s to 3.0 s: flux steady, so **no emf**, however large the flux.
3.0 s to 3.5 s: slope −6.0 mWb s⁻¹, so 6.0 mV per turn in the **opposite** sense.

visual.alt: Flux through one turn of a coil against time: it rises steadily to 3 milliwebers in one and a half seconds, stays level for one and a half seconds, then falls to zero in half a second
visual.caption: The emf per turn is the slope: 2.0 mV, then zero, then 6.0 mV in the opposite sense.

slides.narration: On a graph of flux against time, the induced emf is the slope, not the height. While the flux climbs steadily, each turn has two millivolts. While the flux sits at its largest value, the emf is zero, because nothing is changing. When the flux drops to zero in half a second, the slope is three times as steep and of the opposite sign, so the emf is six millivolts per turn, reversed.

slides.heading: Lenz’s law
slides.body_md: **Lenz’s law:** the induced current flows in the direction that **opposes the change** of flux that produces it.
bullets: Flux increasing: the induced field points **against** the existing field.
Flux decreasing: the induced field points **along** the existing field, trying to keep it.
Pulling a south pole away from a coil makes the near face a **north** pole, which attracts the magnet back.

slides.narration: Lenz’s law gives the direction. The induced current always opposes the change that causes it, not the field itself. In the picture a south pole is being pulled away from a solenoid. The flux it sends through the coil is shrinking, so the induced current tries to keep it, turning the near face into a north pole. That north pole attracts the departing south pole, holding it back.

slides.heading: Lenz’s law and conservation of energy
slides.body_md: Because the induced current always opposes the motion or change, **work must be done** to keep the flux changing. That work is the source of the electrical energy (heat in the circuit).
bullets: If the induced current aided the motion, a small push would make the magnet speed up by itself, producing energy from nothing.
So Lenz’s law is a consequence of the **conservation of energy**.

slides.narration: Why must the current oppose the change? Suppose it helped instead. A magnet nudged towards a coil would be pulled in faster, which would induce more current and pull harder still, heating the coil with no one doing any work. That would create energy from nothing. Because the current opposes, you must push the magnet, and the work you do is exactly what appears as electrical energy.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which way does the current flow?
slides.body_md: A square loop in the plane of the page is pushed into a region where a uniform field points into the page. Find the direction of the induced current while it enters, and while it moves wholly inside.
bullets: Entering: the inward flux grows, so the induced field must point **out of the page**: current **anticlockwise** (seen from the front).
Wholly inside a uniform field: the flux is constant, so there is **no induced current**.
Leaving: the inward flux falls, so the current is **clockwise**, keeping the inward field.

The induced field must point outward, and by the right-hand rule that needs an anticlockwise current as you look at the page. Once the loop is wholly inside the uniform field, the flux stops changing and the current stops. As it leaves, the current turns clockwise.

slides.heading: Motional emf: E = Blv
slides.body_md:
A bar of length $l$ moves with speed $v$ along rails in a field $B$ normal to their plane. If it is a distance $x$ from the closed end, the flux through the circuit is $\Phi = Blx$, so
$$\varepsilon = \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = Bl\dfrac{dx}{dt} = Blv$$
bullets: Same result from forces: each free charge feels $qvB$ along the bar; charges separate until $qE = qvB$, so $\varepsilon = El = Blv$.
Direction from Lenz’s law or from $q\vec v \times \vec B$.

slides.narration: Now move a conductor through a field. As the bar slides, the area of the circuit grows, so the flux grows at the rate B times l times v. That is the motional emf. The same answer comes from forces: the moving free charges in the bar are pushed along it by the magnetic force until the electric field from the separated charges balances them. Here, with the field out of the page, the current flows down the bar.

slides.heading: Force, current and power
slides.body_md:
With circuit resistance $R$: $I = \dfrac{Blv}{R}$. The field exerts a force $F = BIl = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$ on the bar, **opposing** its motion. To keep $v$ constant, an equal force must be applied, supplying power
$$P = Fv = \dfrac{(Blv)^2}{R} = I^2R$$
bullets: Mechanical power in = electrical power out as heat in R: energy is conserved.
Doubling v doubles the emf, the current and the force, and multiplies the power by four.

slides.narration: The induced current in the bar sits in the magnetic field, so it feels a force B I l, and Lenz’s law says this force points backwards. To keep the bar moving steadily, you must push with an equal force. Your power, force times speed, is B l v squared over R, exactly the rate at which heat appears in the resistor. Mechanical energy is turned into electrical energy, and none is created.

Step 2 — $F = BIl = 0.40 \times 1.0 \times 0.50 = 0.20$ N.

slides.narration: The emf is point four times point five times four, point eight volts, and with point eight ohms the current is one ampere. The drag on the bar is B I l, a fifth of a newton, so the pushing force must be the same. The power is force times speed, point eight watts, which matches the emf squared over the resistance. On the graph, the power grows as the square of the speed.

slides.heading: Eddy currents
slides.body_md: When the flux through a **bulk piece of metal** changes (the metal moves in a field, or the field changes), induced currents circulate in closed loops inside it: **eddy currents**.
bullets: Effects: **heating** of the metal and a **force opposing** the relative motion (Lenz’s law).
In transformer and motor cores they waste energy; **lamination** (thin sheets insulated by varnish) breaks the loops into small ones and cuts the loss.
Treated qualitatively in the ISC syllabus.

slides.narration: In a solid block of metal there are no wires to guide the induced current, so it swirls in closed loops inside the metal, like eddies in a stream. These eddy currents heat the metal and, by Lenz’s law, resist any motion of the metal through the field. In machines this heating is wasted energy, so cores are built from thin sheets insulated from one another, which leaves room only for small, weak loops.

slides.heading: Putting eddy currents to work
slides.body_md: The same heating and opposing forces are useful:
bullets: Faster changes give larger eddy currents, so magnetic braking is strongest at high speed and fades smoothly as the vehicle slows.

rows: Large eddy currents heat the metal itself
Force on a moving disc or rail opposes the motion
Currents in the metal frame damp the swinging coil
Drag on a moving disc grows with its speed
Heating loss, reduced by laminating the core

visual.alt: Table of uses and effects of eddy currents: furnaces and cooktops, electromagnetic brakes, dead-beat galvanometers, speedometers and meter discs, and the unwanted heating of cores that lamination reduces

slides.narration: Engineers use eddy currents on purpose. An induction furnace or cooktop heats metal by making large eddy currents flow in it. Metro trains brake by switching on electromagnets near a metal disc or rail. A galvanometer coil wound on a metal frame stops swinging quickly. Speedometers and old energy meters use the drag on a spinning disc. Only in cores are they a nuisance, tamed by lamination.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Induced current opposes the change; follows from energy conservation
Heating and damping; reduced by laminating cores

visual.alt: Summary table of flux, Faraday’s law, Lenz’s law, motional emf, the force and power on a moving bar, and eddy currents

slides.narration: To sum up: flux is B A cos theta, with theta measured from the normal. The induced emf is the rate of change of flux linkage, and the charge that flows depends only on the change. Lenz’s law gives the direction and follows from conservation of energy. A moving bar has an emf B l v, and the power to drive it is B l v squared over R. Eddy currents heat and damp, and laminated cores reduce them.

slides.narration: A coil does not like its current to change. Switch it on and the current creeps up; switch it off and it fights back with a spark. In this part we measure that stubbornness as self-inductance, see how one coil can induce an emf in its neighbour through mutual inductance, and use the idea to build the transformer, the device that makes long-distance power lines possible.

slides.heading: Self-induction
slides.body_md:
The current $I$ in a coil sets up a flux through its own turns. The flux linkage is proportional to the current:
$$N\Phi = LI,\qquad \varepsilon = -L\,\dfrac{dI}{dt}$$
$L$ is the **self-inductance**. Unit: **henry** (1 H = 1 V s A⁻¹ = 1 Wb A⁻¹).
bullets: A coil has 1 H if a current changing at 1 A s⁻¹ induces 1 V across it.
L depends on the number of turns, the size and shape of the coil and the core, not on the current.

The flux linkage is proportional to the current, and the constant of proportionality is the self-inductance L, measured in henries. One henry means that a current changing by one ampere every second induces one volt.

slides.heading: Self-inductance of a long solenoid
slides.body_md:
A long solenoid: $N$ turns, length $l$, area $A$, $n = N/l$. Inside, $B = \mu_0 nI = \dfrac{\mu_0NI}{l}$, so the flux linkage is
$$N\Phi = N\cdot\dfrac{\mu_0NI}{l}\cdot A = LI \;\Rightarrow\; L = \dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l} = \mu_0n^2Al$$
bullets: L ∝ N²: twice the turns on the same length, four times the inductance.
With an iron core of relative permeability $\mu_r$: $L = \mu_0\mu_rN^2A/l$.

slides.narration: For a long solenoid the field inside is mu nought N I over l. Each of the N turns has this field through its area A, so the flux linkage is mu nought N squared A I over l. Dividing by the current gives the self-inductance, mu nought N squared A over l. It grows as the square of the number of turns, and an iron core multiplies it by the relative permeability.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a solenoid and its back emf
slides.body_md: An air-cored solenoid 25 cm long has 500 turns, each of area 4.0 cm². Find its self-inductance, and the average back emf when a current of 3.0 A through it is switched off in 1.0 ms.
bullets: Step 1 — $L = \dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 500^2 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-4}}{0.25} = 5.03 \times 10^{-4}$ H (about 0.50 mH).
Step 2 — $\varepsilon = L\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = 5.03 \times 10^{-4} \times \dfrac{3.0}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.51$ V.

visual.alt: Worked table: self-inductance 0.503 millihenry, current falling at 3000 amperes per second, back emf about 1.5 volts

slides.narration: Put the numbers into mu nought N squared A over l: about half a millihenry, a small inductance because the coil has no iron. Switching off three amperes in a thousandth of a second is a fall of three thousand amperes per second, so the back emf is about one and a half volts. With an iron core, or a faster switch, it could be hundreds of times larger.

slides.heading: Back emf
slides.body_md: The induced emf $-L\,dI/dt$ in a coil is called the **back emf**: it opposes the **change** of current, not the current itself.
bullets: Self-inductance acts like inertia in mechanics: it resists changes of current as mass resists changes of velocity.

rows: Coil acts as a plain resistance
Large, tries to keep the current going

visual.alt: Table of the back emf of a coil when a switch is closed, when the current is steady and when the switch is opened

slides.narration: This emf is called the back emf. When the switch is closed, it opposes the rising current, so the current grows gradually. When the current is steady, it is zero. When the switch is opened, the current tries to fall to zero at once, the back emf becomes very large in the direction that keeps the current going, and a spark may jump across the switch. Inductance behaves like inertia for current.

slides.heading: Mutual induction
slides.body_md:
A current $I_1$ in coil 1 sends flux through coil 2. The flux linkage of coil 2 is proportional to $I_1$:
$$N_2\Phi_2 = MI_1,\qquad \varepsilon_2 = -M\,\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}$$
$M$ is the **mutual inductance** (henry); for a given pair $M_{12} = M_{21}$.
bullets: M is larger for more turns, larger area, closer coils sharing an axis, and an iron core through both.
A steady current in coil 1 induces nothing in coil 2.

slides.narration: Now take two coils. A current in the first sends some of its flux through the second. If that current changes, an emf appears in the second coil, equal to M times the rate of change of the first current. M is the mutual inductance, also measured in henries, and it is the same whichever coil carries the current. It depends on the turns, the areas, how the coils are placed, and any iron core.

slides.heading: Mutual inductance of two coaxial solenoids
slides.body_md:
Inner solenoid: radius $r_1$, $n_1$ turns per metre; outer: $n_2$ turns per metre; common length $l$. A current $I_2$ in the outer gives $B_2 = \mu_0n_2I_2$ through the inner one’s area $\pi r_1^2$. Its $n_1l$ turns link
$$N_1\Phi_1 = (n_1l)(\mu_0n_2I_2)(\pi r_1^2) = MI_2 \;\Rightarrow\; M = \mu_0n_1n_2\pi r_1^2l$$
bullets: Current $I_1$ in the inner solenoid gives the same linkage with the outer one, so $M_{12} = M_{21}$.
Only the inner area $\pi r_1^2$ counts: outside the inner solenoid its field is zero.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: coaxial solenoids
slides.body_md: An inner solenoid of radius 1.0 cm has 1200 turns per metre; the outer one has 800 turns per metre; both are 60 cm long. Find M, and the emf in the inner solenoid when the outer current changes at 50 A s⁻¹.

slides.heading: The transformer
slides.body_md: Two coils, the **primary** (Np turns) and the **secondary** (Ns turns), are wound on a common **laminated soft-iron core**.
bullets: An alternating voltage in the primary drives an alternating current, which sets up an **alternating flux** in the core.
The same changing flux links the secondary and induces an alternating emf in it (**mutual induction**).
A transformer works only with **changing** current: on steady DC the secondary emf is zero.

slides.narration: A transformer is two coils on one iron core. An alternating voltage across the primary drives an alternating current, which magnetises the core first one way and then the other. The iron carries this alternating flux round to the secondary coil, where it induces an alternating emf. Nothing flows from one coil to the other; the energy is carried by the changing flux. With steady direct current, nothing would be induced.

slides.heading: Ideal transformer relations
slides.body_md:
No flux leakage: the same $d\Phi/dt$ in every turn, so $\varepsilon_p = N_p\,d\Phi/dt$ and $\varepsilon_s = N_s\,d\Phi/dt$. No losses: $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$.
$$\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = \dfrac{I_p}{I_s}$$
bullets: **Step-up** ($N_s > N_p$): voltage up, current down.
**Step-down** ($N_s < N_p$): voltage down, current up.
A transformer cannot increase power.

slides.narration: If every turn of both coils carries the same changing flux, each turn has the same emf, so the voltages are in the ratio of the turns. If no energy is lost, the power in equals the power out, so the currents are in the inverse ratio. A step-up transformer raises the voltage and lowers the current; a step-down transformer does the opposite. Neither gives more power than it takes.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a doorbell transformer
slides.body_md: An ideal transformer with 460 primary turns steps 230 V mains down to 6.0 V for a doorbell that draws 1.15 A. Find the number of secondary turns and the primary current.
bullets: Step 1 — $N_s = N_p\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = 460 \times \dfrac{6.0}{230} = 12$ turns.
Step 2 — $I_p = \dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{6.0 \times 1.15}{230} = 0.030$ A (30 mA).

visual.alt: Worked table: primary 460 turns, 230 volts, 0.03 amperes; secondary 12 turns, 6 volts, 1.15 amperes

slides.narration: The voltage falls by a factor of two hundred and thirty over six, so the secondary needs only twelve turns. The power in the secondary is about six point nine watts, and the primary must supply the same at two hundred and thirty volts, which is only thirty milliamperes. The current is stepped up in exactly the ratio the voltage is stepped down.

slides.heading: Efficiency and energy losses
slides.body_md: Efficiency $\eta = \dfrac{\text{output power}}{\text{input power}} = \dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_pI_p}$; large transformers reach 95–99%.
bullets: Most losses appear as heat, which is why large transformers are cooled with oil.

rows: Core magnetised back and forth each cycle
Soft iron or silicon steel core
Not all primary flux links the secondary
Coils wound one over the other

visual.alt: Table of the four energy losses in a transformer, their causes and their remedies: copper loss, eddy-current loss, hysteresis loss and flux leakage

slides.narration: Real transformers are not quite ideal, though large ones come close. Energy is lost as heat in the resistance of the windings, in eddy currents in the core, and in magnetising the core back and forth every cycle, called hysteresis. A little flux also leaks past the secondary. Thick copper wire, a laminated core of soft iron, and coils wound one over the other keep these losses small.

slides.heading: Power transmission
slides.body_md:
A line of resistance $R$ carrying power $P$ at voltage $V$ has current $I = P/V$ and wastes
$$P_{loss} = I^2R = \dfrac{P^2R}{V^2}$$
bullets: Raising V by a factor k cuts the loss by $k^2$; so power is stepped **up** for transmission and **down** near the users for safety.
This needs AC: transformers do not work on steady DC.

visual.alt: Flow of electrical power from a generator at about 11 kilovolts, through a step-up transformer, along a long-distance line at 220 kilovolts or more, through step-down substations, to homes at 230 volts

slides.narration: Long power lines have resistance, and the heat they waste is I squared R. For a fixed power, the current is power divided by voltage, so the loss falls as one over the voltage squared. That is why generators feed a step-up transformer, the line runs at hundreds of kilovolts, and step-down transformers bring it to two hundred and thirty volts near homes, where it is safe to use.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: why high voltage?
slides.body_md: A town takes 500 kW through lines of total resistance 5.0 Ω. Compare the power lost at 11 kV and at 33 kV.
bullets: At 11 kV: $I = \dfrac{500\,000}{11\,000} = 45.5$ A; loss $= I^2R = 10.3$ kW (about 2% of the power).
At 33 kV: $I = 15.2$ A; loss $= 1.15$ kW: **nine times smaller**.

At thirty three kilovolts the current is a third as large, and the loss falls to about one point one five kilowatts, nine times smaller. The graph shows the loss falling steeply as the voltage rises.

visual.alt: Summary table of self-induction, the solenoid formula, mutual induction, coaxial solenoids, the ideal transformer and power transmission

slides.narration: To sum up: a coil’s flux linkage is L times its current, and a changing current gives a back emf, minus L d I by d t. A long solenoid has L equal to mu nought N squared A over l. Two coils share a mutual inductance M, which for coaxial solenoids is mu nought n one n two pi r one squared l. A transformer uses mutual induction to change voltage in the ratio of the turns, and high-voltage transmission cuts line losses.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Back emf depends on dI/dt, not on I: it can be large when I is zero.
In the M derivation, use the area of the INNER solenoid.
Transformer numericals: turns ratio for V, inverse ratio for I, efficiency for real ones.
Losses: name the loss and its remedy as a pair.

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: Remember that a back emf depends on how fast the current changes, not on how large it is. In the coaxial derivation, always use the cross-section of the inner solenoid. In transformer problems, voltages follow the turns ratio and currents the inverse ratio, with the efficiency included for a real transformer. And when asked about losses, give each loss together with how it is reduced.

sections.heading: 1. Magnetic flux and Faraday’s laws
sections.body_md:
- **Magnetic flux** through a flat coil of area A in a uniform field: $\Phi = \vec B \cdot \vec A = BA\cos\theta$, θ between $\vec B$ and the **normal**. Unit: weber, 1 Wb = 1 T m². Flux linkage of N turns: $N\Phi$.
- If the angle is given from the **plane** of the coil, use θ = 90° minus that angle.
- **First law:** an emf is induced whenever the flux linked with a circuit changes, and only while it changes. **Second law:** $\varepsilon = -N\,\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$ (the minus sign is Lenz’s law).
- The flux can change through B, A or θ. On a Φ–t graph the emf per turn is the (negative) **slope**: a steady flux, however large, gives no emf.
- Charge that flows round a closed coil of resistance R: $q = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R}$, independent of how fast the change happens.

sections.heading: 2. Lenz’s law and motional emf
sections.body_md:
- **Lenz’s law:** the induced current flows so as to **oppose the change** of flux that produces it (not the flux itself). Flux increasing: induced field against B; flux decreasing: induced field along B.
- Steps: (1) is the flux through the loop increasing or decreasing, and which way does it point? (2) choose the induced field that opposes the change; (3) right-hand rule for the current.
- Lenz’s law follows from **conservation of energy**: because the induced current opposes the motion, work must be done, and that work becomes the electrical energy.
- **Motional emf:** a bar of length l moving at v on rails in a perpendicular field: $\Phi = Blx$, so $\varepsilon = Bl\,\dfrac{dx}{dt} = Blv$. Same result from forces: $qvB$ on each free charge balances $qE$, so $\varepsilon = El = Blv$.
- With circuit resistance R: $I = Blv/R$; opposing force $F = BIl = B^2l^2v/R$; power to keep v steady $P = Fv = (Blv)^2/R = I^2R$.

sections.heading: 3. Eddy currents (qualitative)
sections.body_md:
- **Eddy currents** are induced currents circulating in closed loops inside a bulk conductor when the flux through it changes (the metal moves in a field or the field changes).
- **Effects:** heating of the metal; a force that **opposes** the relative motion (Lenz’s law).
- **Uses:** induction furnaces and cooktops (heating); electromagnetic brakes on trains; dead-beat galvanometers (damping by the metal frame); speedometers and energy-meter discs.
- **Unwanted:** heating of transformer and motor cores. **Lamination** (thin sheets insulated by varnish) confines the eddy currents to small, high-resistance paths and reduces the loss. Slots cut in a plate do the same.
- ISC treats eddy currents qualitatively only.

key_terms.definition_md: Induced currents that circulate inside a bulk piece of metal when the flux through it changes.
Building a core from thin sheets insulated from one another to reduce eddy currents.

sections.heading: 4. Self-induction
sections.body_md:
- The flux linkage of a coil is proportional to its own current: $N\Phi = LI$, and $\varepsilon = -L\,\dfrac{dI}{dt}$. **Self-inductance** L, unit **henry** (1 H = 1 Wb A⁻¹ = 1 V s A⁻¹).
- **Long solenoid** (N turns, length l, area A, n = N/l): $B = \mu_0NI/l$, $N\Phi = \mu_0N^2AI/l$, so $L = \dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l} = \mu_0n^2Al$; with a core $\mu_r$ times larger.
- L depends on the turns, size, shape and core, **not** on the current.
- **Back emf** opposes the **change** of current: the current grows gradually when switched on; a large emf (spark) appears when it is switched off. It depends on dI/dt, so it can be large when I is zero. Inductance is “electrical inertia”.

key_terms.definition_md: Flux linkage of a coil per unit current through it, L = NΦ/I; unit henry.
The emf −L dI/dt induced in a coil by a change of its own current.

sections.heading: 5. Mutual induction
sections.body_md:
- A current $I_1$ in coil 1 links flux with coil 2: $N_2\Phi_2 = MI_1$ and $\varepsilon_2 = -M\,\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}$. **Mutual inductance** M, in henry; $M_{12} = M_{21}$.
- M grows with the turns and areas, with closer, coaxial placing and with a soft-iron core through both coils.
- **Coaxial solenoids** (inner radius $r_1$, $n_1$ and $n_2$ turns per metre, common length l): the outer field $\mu_0n_2I_2$ passes through the inner area $\pi r_1^2$ and links $n_1l$ turns, so $M = \mu_0n_1n_2\pi r_1^2l$. Only the **inner** area counts.

sections.heading: 6. The transformer and power transmission
sections.body_md:
- **Principle:** mutual induction. Primary ($N_p$) and secondary ($N_s$) on a laminated soft-iron core; the alternating primary current sets up an alternating flux that links the secondary. It does not work on steady DC.
- **Ideal** (no flux leakage, no losses): $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = \dfrac{I_p}{I_s}$. Step-up: $N_s > N_p$; step-down: $N_s < N_p$. It never increases power.
- **Efficiency** $\eta = \dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_pI_p}$ (95–99% for large transformers). **Losses:** copper ($I^2R$; thick wire), eddy currents (laminated core), hysteresis (soft iron or silicon steel), flux leakage (windings one over the other).
- **Transmission:** line loss $I^2R = \dfrac{P^2R}{V^2}$; raising V k times cuts the loss $k^2$ times. Power is stepped up for long lines and stepped down to 230 V, 50 Hz near users.

questions.stem_md: A 500-turn search coil sits in the gap of an electromagnet whose field has been held steady at 1.2 T for several minutes. The emf across the coil is

options.text_md: large, since the field through the coil is strong
proportional to 500 × 1.2 T, the turns times the field
zero, since the flux through the coil is not changing
equal to the flux linkage of the coil divided by its resistance

questions.solution_md: An emf is induced only while the flux linkage changes. A steady field, however strong, gives dΦ/dt = 0 and so no emf — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A square loop of side 15 cm lies in a uniform magnetic field of 0.40 T, with the plane of the loop at 30° to the field. Find the magnetic flux through the loop, in mWb.
questions.solution_md: The normal makes $\theta = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$ with $\vec B$. $\Phi = BA\cos\theta = 0.40 \times (0.15)^2 \times 0.50 = 4.5 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb, i.e. $4.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{3} = 4.5$ mWb.

marking_scheme.step: θ = 60° from the normal; Φ = 4.5 mWb

questions.stem_md: If the flux linked with a single loop of wire changes steadily by one ___ every second, the emf induced in the loop is one volt.
questions.solution_md: One **weber** per second: by Faraday’s law the emf is the rate of change of flux, and 1 Wb s⁻¹ = 1 V.

questions.stem_md: A 200-turn coil, each turn of area 25 cm², has its plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.30 T. The field is reversed, to 0.30 T in the opposite direction, in 15 ms. Find the average emf induced in the coil, in volts.
questions.solution_md: The flux per turn goes from $+BA$ to $-BA$: $\Delta\Phi = 2BA = 2 \times 0.30 \times 25 \times 10^{-4} = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb. $\varepsilon = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{200 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-3}}{0.015} = 20$ V.

questions.stem_md: The field through a 120-turn coil of area 40 cm², whose normal lies along the field, varies as B = (0.80 − 0.10t²) T, with t in seconds. Find the magnitude of the emf induced in the coil at t = 2.0 s, in volts (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{dB}{dt} = -0.20t$, which at $t = 2.0$ s is $-0.40$ T s$^{-1}$. $|\varepsilon| = NA\left|\dfrac{dB}{dt}\right| = 120 \times 40 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.40 = 0.192$ V. (The field is falling, so by Lenz’s law the induced current tries to keep it.)

marking_scheme.step: dB/dt = −0.40 T s⁻¹ at t = 2.0 s

questions.stem_md: A search coil of 40 turns, each of area 2.0 cm², is connected to a charge meter; the total resistance of the circuit is 80 Ω. The coil, held with its plane perpendicular to the field in the gap of a magnet where B = 0.60 T, is snatched out to a place where the field is negligible. Find the charge that flows, in μC.
questions.solution_md: $q = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R} = \dfrac{40 \times 0.60 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-4}}{80} = 6.0 \times 10^{-5}$ C, i.e. $6.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^{6} = 60$ μC, however quickly the coil is removed.

questions.stem_md: The flux through each turn of a 25-turn coil rises at a steady rate from zero to 6.0 mWb in 0.30 s and then stays at 6.0 mWb. While the flux is rising, the emf across the whole coil is

options.text_md: 20 mV
zero, since the flux settles at a steady value

questions.solution_md: $\varepsilon = N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = 25 \times \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{-3}}{0.30} = 0.50$ V. 20 mV is the emf of one turn; 0.15 V forgets to divide by the time; the emf is zero only after the flux stops changing — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Coil P has 100 turns, each of area A. Coil Q has 300 turns, each of area A/2. Both lie with their planes perpendicular to the same uniform field, which is changing steadily. The ratio of the emf in P to the emf in Q is
questions.solution_md: $\varepsilon = NA\,\dfrac{dB}{dt}$, so $\dfrac{\varepsilon_P}{\varepsilon_Q} = \dfrac{100A}{300 \times A/2} = \dfrac{100}{150} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Whether a magnet is withdrawn slowly or quickly from a closed coil, the same total charge flows round the coil.

**Reason (R):** The emf induced in the coil is larger when the magnet is withdrawn more quickly.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R does not explain A. The charge is q = NΔΦ/R, which depends only on the total change of flux and the resistance; a quicker change gives a larger emf and current for a shorter time — option (b).

questions.stem_md: State Faraday’s first and second laws of electromagnetic induction, and write the second law as an equation for a coil of N turns.

answer.model_answer_md: **First law:** an emf is induced in a circuit whenever the magnetic flux linked with it changes, and it lasts only while the change continues. **Second law:** the induced emf equals the rate of change of the flux linkage: $\varepsilon = -N\,\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$, where the minus sign expresses Lenz’s law.

questions.solution_md: Changing flux linkage induces an emf; ε = −N dΦ/dt.

marking_scheme.step: First law: emf while the flux linkage changes

questions.stem_md: A coil is joined to a galvanometer. Without moving any magnet, describe three different ways of making a current flow in the coil, naming the quantity in Φ = BA cos θ that changes in each.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Switch the current on or off in a nearby electromagnet, so that **B** changes. (ii) Squeeze or stretch the coil, if it is flexible, to change its **area A**. (iii) Rotate the coil in a steady field so that the **angle θ** changes. Each changes the flux, and a current flows only while the change happens.

questions.solution_md: Change B, A or θ.

marking_scheme.step: Any two of the three ways, with the changing quantity
The third way, and the current lasts only during the change

questions.stem_md: The flux through each turn of a 40-turn coil rises steadily from zero to 8.0 mWb between t = 0 and t = 2.0 s, stays at 8.0 mWb until t = 5.0 s, and then changes steadily to −4.0 mWb (the reverse direction) by t = 6.0 s. Find the emf across the coil in each of the three intervals and compare their directions.

answer.model_answer_md:
0 to 2.0 s: $\varepsilon = N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{40 \times 8.0 \times 10^{-3}}{2.0} = 0.16$ V.
2.0 s to 5.0 s: the flux is constant, so $\varepsilon = 0$.
5.0 s to 6.0 s: $\Delta\Phi = -4.0 - 8.0 = -12$ mWb, so $|\varepsilon| = \dfrac{40 \times 12 \times 10^{-3}}{1.0} = 0.48$ V, three times the first value and in the **opposite** direction, because the flux now decreases instead of increasing.

questions.solution_md: emf = N × slope of the Φ–t graph.

marking_scheme.step: 0.48 V, opposite direction, in the third

questions.stem_md: Show that the charge that flows round a closed coil of N turns and resistance R, when the flux through each turn changes by ΔΦ, is NΔΦ/R whatever the time taken. A 150-turn coil of area 12 cm² and resistance 9.0 Ω has its plane perpendicular to a 0.25 T field; it is turned until its plane is parallel to the field. Find the charge that flows.

answer.model_answer_md:
At any instant $I = \dfrac{|\varepsilon|}{R} = \dfrac{N}{R}\left|\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}\right|$, so $dq = I\,dt = \dfrac{N}{R}|d\Phi|$. Adding over the whole change, $q = \dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R}$: the time cancels.
Here the flux per turn falls from $BA$ to zero: $\Delta\Phi = 0.25 \times 12 \times 10^{-4} = 3.0 \times 10^{-4}$ Wb, so $q = \dfrac{150 \times 3.0 \times 10^{-4}}{9.0} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ C (5.0 mC).

questions.solution_md: dq = I dt = (N/R) dΦ.

marking_scheme.step: I dt = (N/R) dΦ, so q = NΔΦ/R

questions.stem_md: A rectangular loop in the plane of the page is being pulled out of a region where a uniform magnetic field points into the page. Seen from the front, the current induced in the loop

options.text_md: flows clockwise, trying to keep the inward flux through the loop
flows anticlockwise, opposing the inward field
is zero, because the field in the region is uniform
flows clockwise in one half of the loop and anticlockwise in the other

questions.solution_md: The inward flux through the loop is decreasing, so the induced field must point into the page to oppose the decrease. By the right-hand rule that needs a clockwise current as seen from the front — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A light aluminium ring hangs from a thread with its plane vertical. The north pole of a bar magnet is moved quickly towards the ring along its axis. The ring

options.text_md: swings away from the approaching magnet
swings towards the approaching magnet
stays still, because aluminium is not attracted by magnets
turns until its plane lies along the magnet

questions.solution_md: The flux through the ring grows, so the induced current makes the near face of the ring a north pole, which repels the approaching north pole: the ring swings away — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A long straight wire in the plane of the page carries a current towards the top of the page. A rectangular loop lies in the page to the left of the wire. The current in the wire is steadily reduced. Seen from the front, the current induced in the loop is

options.text_md: clockwise
zero, since the loop does not move
clockwise at first, then anticlockwise
anticlockwise

questions.solution_md: To the left of a wire carrying current up the page, the field points out of the page. That outward flux is decreasing, so the induced field must also point out of the page, which needs an anticlockwise current seen from the front — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? When the current in a long straight wire is switched off, the current induced in a nearby closed loop flows so as to keep up, for a moment, the flux that the wire had been sending through the loop.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. The flux through the loop is falling, so by Lenz’s law the induced current sets up a field in the same direction as the wire’s field, opposing the decrease.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Pushing a bar magnet towards a closed copper coil takes more effort than pushing it at the same speed towards an identical coil whose wire has been cut.

**Reason (R):** The current induced in the closed coil sets up a magnetic field that repels the approaching magnet.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: only the closed coil carries an induced current, and by Lenz’s law its field repels the magnet, so extra work is needed; the cut coil has an emf but no current — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An inventor claims to have designed a coil in which the induced current helps a magnet move towards the coil, so that the magnet speeds up by itself while the coil warms up. Evaluate the claim using Lenz’s law.

answer.model_answer_md: The claim must be **false**. If the induced current aided the motion, the magnet would gain kinetic energy and the coil would gain heat with **no work done** by anyone: energy would be created from nothing. Conservation of energy requires the induced current to **oppose** the change (Lenz’s law), so work must be done to move the magnet.

questions.solution_md: Aiding current would create energy from nothing.

marking_scheme.step: Aiding current would give energy with no work done
Energy conservation requires opposition (Lenz’s law): claim false

questions.stem_md: A car with a vertical radio antenna 0.90 m long drives due east at 25 m s⁻¹. The horizontal component of the Earth’s magnetic field there is 3.6 × 10⁻⁵ T, pointing north. Find the emf between the ends of the antenna, in mV.
questions.solution_md: The antenna, its velocity and the horizontal field are mutually perpendicular, so $\varepsilon = Blv = 3.6 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.90 \times 25 = 8.1 \times 10^{-4}$ V, i.e. $8.1 \times 10^{-4} \times 10^{3} = 0.81$ mV. ($\vec v \times \vec B$ points upwards, so the top end is positive; the vertical component of the field pushes charges sideways, not along the antenna.)

questions.stem_md: A conducting bar 0.48 m long slides at 2.5 m s⁻¹ along rails joined by a 0.20 Ω resistor, in a uniform field of 0.25 T perpendicular to the plane of the rails. The bar and rails have negligible resistance. Find the current, in amperes.
questions.solution_md: $\varepsilon = Blv = 0.25 \times 0.48 \times 2.5 = 0.30$ V; $I = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{R} = \dfrac{0.30}{0.20} = 1.5$ A.

questions.stem_md: A bar 25 cm long is pulled along rails in a uniform field of 0.60 T perpendicular to their plane; the circuit resistance is 0.45 Ω. At what steady speed must it move for the resistor to dissipate 1.25 W? Answer in m s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: $P = \dfrac{(Blv)^2}{R}$, so $Blv = \sqrt{PR} = \sqrt{1.25 \times 0.45} = 0.75$ V and $v = \dfrac{0.75}{0.60 \times 0.25} = 5.0$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: A bar is kept moving at a steady speed along rails joined by a resistor, in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the rails. The field is doubled, while the speed and the resistance stay the same. The force needed to keep the bar moving and the power supplied by the agent become

options.text_md: force × 2, power × 2
force × 4, power × 4
force × 2, power × 4
force × 4, power × 2

questions.solution_md: $F = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$ and $P = Fv = \dfrac{B^2l^2v^2}{R}$: both vary as $B^2$, so both become four times as large — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A metal rod moving along its own length through a uniform magnetic field has an emf induced between its ends.

**Reason (R):** The magnetic force on a free charge carried along by the rod is perpendicular to the rod’s velocity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true: F = qv × B is perpendicular to v. A is false: when v is along the rod, that force is perpendicular to the rod, so no charge is pushed from one end to the other and there is no emf between the ends (the rod also sweeps out no area) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A bar lying across smooth horizontal rails, joined at one end through a resistor, sits in a vertical magnetic field. It is given a quick push along the rails and released. Describe its motion and say what becomes of its kinetic energy.

answer.model_answer_md: The moving bar has a motional emf **Blv**, so a current flows and the field exerts a force **B²l²v/R** on the bar that **opposes its motion** (Lenz’s law). The bar slows down, ever more gently as v falls, and comes to rest. Its kinetic energy is turned into **heat** in the resistor and the bar.

questions.solution_md: Drag ∝ v slows it; KE → heat.

marking_scheme.step: Induced current gives a drag force opposing the motion: bar slows and stops
Kinetic energy becomes heat in the circuit

questions.stem_md: A straight conductor of length l moves with velocity v perpendicular to itself and to a uniform magnetic field B. Using the magnetic force on its free charges, show that the emf between its ends is Blv. If the conductor lies north–south, moves east, and the field points vertically upwards, which end is at the higher potential?

answer.model_answer_md:
Each free charge $q$ moves with the conductor and feels $\vec F = q\vec v \times \vec B$, of size $qvB$, along the conductor. Charges pile up at the ends until the electric field $E$ they create balances this force: $qE = qvB$, so $E = vB$. The p.d. between the ends, which is the emf, is $\varepsilon = El = Blv$.
With $\vec v$ east and $\vec B$ up, $\vec v \times \vec B$ points **south**, so positive charges are pushed to the south end: the **south end** is at the higher potential.

questions.solution_md: qE = qvB; ε = El = Blv; v × B points south.

marking_scheme.step: Force qvB along the conductor separates charges
qE = qvB, so ε = El = Blv
v × B is south: south end at higher potential

questions.stem_md: A single square loop of wire of side 10 cm and resistance 0.020 Ω lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.80 T. It is pulled out of the field at a steady 0.50 m s⁻¹, one side leaving first. Find (a) the emf and current while it leaves, (b) the force needed, (c) the work done in pulling it completely out, and show that this equals the heat produced.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Only one side cuts the field lines: $\varepsilon = Blv = 0.80 \times 0.10 \times 0.50 = 0.040$ V; $I = \dfrac{0.040}{0.020} = 2.0$ A.
(b) The side still in the field feels $F = BIl = 0.80 \times 2.0 \times 0.10 = 0.16$ N opposing the motion, so an equal pull is needed.
(c) $W = Fd = 0.16 \times 0.10 = 0.016$ J. The loop takes $\dfrac{0.10}{0.50} = 0.20$ s to leave, and the heat is $I^2Rt = 2.0^2 \times 0.020 \times 0.20 = 0.016$ J, the same.

questions.solution_md: ε = Blv; F = BIl; W = Fd = I²Rt.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Eddy currents can flow in a metal sheet that is held perfectly still, provided the magnetic flux through the sheet is changing.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Any change of flux through a conductor induces eddy currents: the metal may move through a steady field, or stay still in a changing field (as in a transformer core or under an induction cooktop).

questions.stem_md: The armature core of an electric motor is assembled from thin steel stampings, each coated with varnish, rather than machined from one solid block of steel. The main purpose is to

options.text_md: stop the magnetic flux from passing through the core
make the core more strongly magnetised by the winding current
reduce the I²R heating in the copper windings
confine the eddy currents to thin sheets, where their paths have a high resistance, cutting the heating loss

questions.solution_md: The varnish insulates the stampings from one another, so eddy currents can circulate only within each thin sheet; these small paths carry far smaller currents and waste far less heat. The flux still passes along the sheets — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A flat copper plate hangs as a pendulum and swings between the poles of an electromagnet. When the electromagnet is switched on, the plate

options.text_md: is pulled to one pole and sticks there, as copper is strongly magnetic
swings with a larger amplitude, as the field adds energy to it
stops swinging within a few swings, as eddy currents turn its energy into heat
swings exactly as before, because copper is not magnetic

questions.solution_md: As the plate moves through the field, eddy currents are induced in it; by Lenz’s law they oppose the motion, so the swing is damped and its energy appears as heat in the plate — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A copper plate with deep slots cut across it swings much more freely between the poles of a magnet than a solid copper plate of the same size.

**Reason (R):** The slots break up the paths of the eddy currents, so the currents and the opposing force are much smaller.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: with the eddy-current loops broken by the slots, much less current flows, so the damping force that opposes the swing is much smaller — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A galvanometer whose coil, wound on a metal frame, settles at once without oscillating, because eddy currents in the frame damp its swing, is called a ___ galvanometer.
questions.solution_md: A **dead-beat** galvanometer: eddy currents in the metal frame oppose the motion of the coil and stop it at its final deflection.

questions.stem_md: Match each device in Column A with the part that eddy currents play in it, in Column B.

options.text_md: Induction cooktop
Electromagnetic brake of a metro train
Dead-beat galvanometer
Transformer core

match_right.text_md: Currents in the metal frame of the coil stop it from oscillating
Currents induced in the base of the pan heat the pan directly
Unwanted heating, kept small by building the core from insulated sheets
Currents induced in a moving disc or rail produce a force that slows it

questions.solution_md: Cooktop → heating the pan (1 → q); brake → force opposing the motion (2 → s); dead-beat galvanometer → damping by the frame (3 → p); transformer core → unwanted heating reduced by lamination (4 → r).

questions.stem_md: An induction cooktop heats a steel pan placed on it but hardly warms a glass dish of water. Explain this, and why the cooktop coil carries a current that alternates many thousands of times a second.

answer.model_answer_md: The coil under the glass top makes a rapidly **changing magnetic field**. In the conducting base of the steel pan this induces large **eddy currents**, which heat the metal directly. Glass is an insulator, so no eddy currents flow in the dish. A **faster** change of flux induces a larger emf and so larger eddy currents and more heat.

questions.solution_md: Eddy currents only in conductors; faster change, more heating.

marking_scheme.step: Changing field induces eddy currents in the metal pan; none in glass (insulator)
High frequency: faster change gives larger eddy currents

questions.stem_md: Metro trains do most of their braking with eddy-current brakes, but they still carry ordinary friction brakes. Evaluate why the eddy-current brake alone cannot hold a stopped train on a slope.

answer.model_answer_md: An eddy-current brake needs **relative motion**: the eddy currents and the opposing force grow with the **speed** of the disc or rail. As the train slows the force fades, and at rest it is **zero**, so it cannot hold the train on a slope. Friction brakes are still needed to stop and hold it.

questions.solution_md: Eddy-current force ∝ speed; zero at rest.

marking_scheme.step: Braking force needs motion and falls with speed
Zero at rest, so friction brakes are needed to hold the train

questions.stem_md: What are eddy currents and how are they produced? Give one harmful effect and one useful application of eddy currents, and explain how laminating the core of a transformer reduces the harmful effect.

answer.model_answer_md: Eddy currents are **induced currents** that circulate in closed loops inside a bulk piece of metal when the magnetic flux through it **changes**, because the metal moves in a field or the field itself changes. **Harmful:** they heat the iron cores of transformers and motors, wasting energy. **Useful:** an induction furnace or cooktop heats metal with them (or a train’s electromagnetic brake). **Lamination:** the core is built from thin sheets insulated by varnish, so the eddy currents can only circulate in small loops of high resistance within each sheet, and the heat produced is much smaller.

questions.solution_md: Induced loops in bulk metal; heating loss; furnace or brake; lamination breaks the loops.

marking_scheme.step: Definition and cause (changing flux through bulk metal)
One harmful effect and one use
Lamination confines currents to thin, high-resistance sheets

questions.stem_md: An air-cored solenoid is gently stretched to twice its length, keeping the same number of turns and the same cross-section, and remaining long compared with its width. Its self-inductance

options.text_md: is halved
is doubled
is unchanged
becomes a quarter of its value

questions.solution_md: $L = \dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l}$: with N and A fixed, doubling l halves L (the turns are more widely spaced, so the field and the flux are halved) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A coil has a self-inductance of one ___ if a current through it changing at one ampere per second induces a back emf of one volt across it.
questions.solution_md: One **henry**: 1 H = 1 V s A⁻¹ = 1 Wb A⁻¹.

questions.stem_md: A choke is wound as a single-layer air-cored solenoid of 2400 turns over a length of 30 cm on a former of radius 1.5 cm. Treating it as a long solenoid, find its self-inductance, in mH (3 significant figures).
The current through a coil of self-inductance 250 mH grows steadily from 0.40 A to 1.60 A in 30 ms. Find the size of the back emf, in volts.
questions.solution_md: $|\varepsilon| = L\dfrac{\Delta I}{\Delta t} = 0.25 \times \dfrac{1.20}{0.030} = 10$ V, opposing the rise of current.

questions.stem_md: A coil of negligible resistance is connected in a circuit where its current changes at a steady 40 A s⁻¹. A voltmeter across the coil reads 3.2 V. Find the self-inductance of the coil, in mH.
questions.solution_md: $L = \dfrac{\varepsilon}{dI/dt} = \dfrac{3.2}{40} = 0.080$ H, i.e. $0.080 \times 10^{3} = 80$ mH.

questions.stem_md: A current of 0.50 A in a coil of 400 turns sets up a flux of 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ Wb through each turn. Find the self-inductance of the coil, in mH.
Two long air-cored solenoids P and Q have the same length. Q has three times as many turns as P, and half its radius. The self-inductance of Q is

options.text_md: 3/2 times that of P
3/4 of that of P
9 times that of P
9/4 times that of P

questions.solution_md: $L = \dfrac{\mu_0N^2\pi r^2}{l} \propto N^2r^2$, so $\dfrac{L_Q}{L_P} = 3^2 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{9}{4}$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The back emf across a coil can be large at an instant when the current through the coil is zero.

**Reason (R):** The back emf of a coil depends on the rate of change of the current through it, not on the current itself.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: ε = −L dI/dt. Just after a switch is closed the current is zero but rising fastest, so the back emf is at its largest — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two identical lamps are connected in parallel to a battery through a single switch: lamp X in series with a large iron-cored coil, and lamp Y in series with a resistor equal to the resistance of the coil. Which lamp reaches full brightness later after the switch is closed? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: **Lamp X**. As the current through the coil starts to grow, its self-inductance produces a **back emf** that opposes the rise, so the current in X grows gradually and X brightens slowly. The resistor has no such effect, so Y lights at once. Once the current is steady the back emf is zero, and both lamps are **equally bright**.

questions.solution_md: Back emf of the coil delays the rise of current in X.

marking_scheme.step: Back emf opposes the growth of current; equal brightness when steady

questions.stem_md: Define self-inductance. A long solenoid has n turns per unit length, cross-sectional area A and length l, and is wound on a core of relative permeability μr. Obtain its self-inductance, and state how it changes if n is doubled with l and A unchanged.

answer.model_answer_md:
Self-inductance is the flux linkage of a coil per unit current through it: $N\Phi = LI$ (equivalently the back emf per unit rate of change of current, $\varepsilon = -L\,dI/dt$).
Inside the solenoid $B = \mu_0\mu_r nI$, so the flux through each turn is $\mu_0\mu_r nIA$. There are $nl$ turns, so the flux linkage is $nl \times \mu_0\mu_r nIA = LI$, giving $L = \mu_0\mu_r n^2Al$.
Since $L \propto n^2$, doubling n makes L **four times** as large.

questions.solution_md: NΦ = LI with B = μ₀μr nI.

marking_scheme.step: B = μ₀μr nI; linkage nl × BA
L = μ₀μr n²Al; four times for 2n

questions.stem_md: A coil of self-inductance 0.15 H and resistance 6.0 Ω is connected through a switch to a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance. Find (a) the final steady current, (b) the rate at which the current grows at the instant the switch is closed, (c) the rate of growth when the current has reached 1.0 A.

answer.model_answer_md:
At every instant the battery emf is shared between the back emf and the resistance: $E = L\dfrac{dI}{dt} + IR$.
(a) When steady, $dI/dt = 0$: $I = \dfrac{E}{R} = \dfrac{12}{6.0} = 2.0$ A.
(b) At switch-on $I = 0$: $\dfrac{dI}{dt} = \dfrac{E}{L} = \dfrac{12}{0.15} = 80$ A s$^{-1}$.
(c) At $I = 1.0$ A: $\dfrac{dI}{dt} = \dfrac{12 - 1.0 \times 6.0}{0.15} = 40$ A s$^{-1}$; the growth slows as the current rises.

questions.solution_md: E = L dI/dt + IR.

questions.stem_md: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 1.5 mH. Find the flux linkage of the second coil when a steady current of 4.0 A flows in the first, in mWb.
questions.solution_md: $N_2\Phi_2 = MI_1 = 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 4.0 = 6.0 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb, i.e. $6.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^{3} = 6.0$ mWb (no emf, since the current is steady).

questions.stem_md: A solenoid of 300 turns and radius 2.0 cm lies coaxially inside a wider solenoid of 1500 turns; both are 50 cm long. Find their mutual inductance, in mH (3 significant figures).

marking_scheme.step: M = μ₀N₁N₂πr₁²/l with the inner radius

questions.stem_md: In a car’s ignition coil the mutual inductance between the primary and secondary windings is 4.0 H. A primary current of 3.0 A is cut off steadily in 1.0 ms. Find the emf induced in the secondary, in kV.
questions.solution_md: $|\varepsilon_2| = M\dfrac{\Delta I_1}{\Delta t} = 4.0 \times \dfrac{3.0}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 12000$ V, i.e. $\dfrac{12000}{10^{3}} = 12$ kV, enough to make the spark plug fire.

questions.stem_md: In obtaining M = μ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l for a narrow solenoid of radius r₁ inside a wide coaxial solenoid of radius r₂, the area πr₁² is used and not πr₂², because

options.text_md: the inner solenoid always has more turns per metre than the outer one
only the inner area is linked with both coils: the outer coil’s field fills it, and the inner coil’s field is negligible outside it
the field of the outer solenoid is zero inside the inner solenoid
the region between the two solenoids carries a field in the opposite direction

questions.solution_md: With current in the outer coil, its field passes through each inner turn only over the area πr₁². With current in the inner coil, its field is confined to its own cross-section, so the outer turns also link flux only through πr₁². Either way M = μ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two long coaxial solenoids have mutual inductance M = μ₀n₁n₂πr₁²l. The inner solenoid is replaced by one of twice the radius (still inside the outer one) with half as many turns per metre. The mutual inductance

options.text_md: is unchanged
halves
doubles
becomes four times as large

questions.solution_md: $M \propto n_1r_1^2$: $\dfrac{1}{2} \times 2^2 = 2$, so M doubles — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Winding two coils on a common soft-iron core increases their mutual inductance.

**Reason (R):** The mutual inductance of two coils depends on the current flowing in the first coil.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: soft iron has a large relative permeability, so far more flux from one coil links the other for the same current. R is false: M depends only on the turns, sizes, placing and core of the coils, not on the current — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Define the mutual inductance of a pair of coils in two ways, using (i) the flux linkage of the second coil, (ii) the emf induced in the second coil, and give its SI unit.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) M is the flux linkage of the second coil per unit current in the first coil: $N_2\Phi_2 = MI_1$. (ii) M is the emf induced in the second coil per unit rate of change of current in the first coil: $\varepsilon_2 = -M\,\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}$. Its SI unit is the **henry** (H), equal to one weber per ampere.

questions.solution_md: N₂Φ₂ = MI₁; ε₂ = −M dI₁/dt; henry.

questions.stem_md: A long air-cored solenoid of length l has N₁ turns of radius r₁. A second coil of N₂ turns, also of length l, is wound closely over it. Starting from the field inside a long solenoid, show that their mutual inductance is μ₀N₁N₂πr₁²/l, and explain why the result is the same whichever coil carries the current.

answer.model_answer_md:
A current $I_1$ in the inner solenoid gives a uniform field $B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0N_1I_1}{l}$ over its cross-section $\pi r_1^2$ and practically none outside. Each turn of the outer coil links flux $B_1\pi r_1^2$, so $N_2\Phi_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0N_1N_2\pi r_1^2}{l}I_1 = MI_1$, giving $M = \dfrac{\mu_0N_1N_2\pi r_1^2}{l}$.
With current $I_2$ in the outer coil instead, $B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0N_2I_2}{l}$ fills the inner coil, whose $N_1$ turns link $\dfrac{\mu_0N_1N_2\pi r_1^2}{l}I_2$: the same M, because only the shared area $\pi r_1^2$ is linked either way.

questions.solution_md: B₁ = μ₀N₁I₁/l; linkage over πr₁²; reverse roles.

marking_scheme.step: Same with current in the outer coil: only πr₁² linked

questions.stem_md: When the current in coil P rises steadily from zero to 5.0 A in 0.10 s, an emf of 0.60 V is induced in a nearby coil Q. Find (a) the mutual inductance, (b) the flux linkage of Q when P carries a steady 3.0 A, (c) the emf induced in Q if the 5.0 A current in P is then switched off steadily in 25 ms.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\dfrac{dI}{dt} = \dfrac{5.0}{0.10} = 50$ A s$^{-1}$, so $M = \dfrac{0.60}{50} = 0.012$ H (12 mH).
(b) $N_Q\Phi_Q = MI = 0.012 \times 3.0 = 0.036$ Wb.
(c) $\dfrac{dI}{dt} = \dfrac{5.0}{0.025} = 200$ A s$^{-1}$, so $|\varepsilon| = 0.012 \times 200 = 2.4$ V, in the opposite sense to the emf in (a).

questions.solution_md: M = ε/(dI/dt); NΦ = MI.

questions.stem_md: A step-up transformer for a neon sign raises 230 V mains to 4.6 kV. Its primary has 150 turns. Assuming it is ideal, how many turns does its secondary have?
questions.solution_md: $N_s = N_p\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = 150 \times \dfrac{4600}{230} = 3000$ turns.

questions.stem_md: By mistake, the primary of a mains transformer is connected to a 12 V car battery. Once the switch has been closed for a few seconds, the voltage across the secondary is

options.text_md: 12 V multiplied by Ns/Np
12 V, the same as across the primary
12 V multiplied by Np/Ns
zero

questions.solution_md: A steady current sets up a steady flux in the core, and a steady flux induces no emf in the secondary. (Only a brief pulse appears at the instant of switching; meanwhile the primary, limited only by its small resistance, may overheat) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A transformer for a set of 12 V garden lights runs from 230 V mains and supplies 4.0 A to the lights. Its efficiency is 96%. Find the current drawn from the mains, in amperes (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Output power $= 12 \times 4.0 = 48$ W; input power $= \dfrac{48}{0.96} = 50$ W; $I_p = \dfrac{50}{230} = 0.217$ A.

questions.stem_md: A transformer delivers 855 W to its load, while its copper and core losses together waste 45 W. Find its efficiency, as a percentage.
questions.solution_md: Input $= 855 + 45 = 900$ W, so $\eta = \dfrac{855}{900} \times 100 = 95$ per cent.

questions.stem_md: An ideal transformer with 2000 turns on its primary and 100 turns on its secondary is connected to 230 V mains. Its secondary supplies a heater of resistance 4.6 Ω. Find the current in the primary, in amperes.
The secondary winding of a step-down transformer in a welding set is made of much thicker wire than its primary. This is because the secondary

options.text_md: has a much higher voltage across it, so it needs thicker insulation
carries a much larger current, and thick wire keeps its I²R heating small
must carry more power than the primary supplies
has more turns than the primary, so its wire must be stronger

questions.solution_md: In a step-down transformer Is/Ip = Np/Ns > 1: the secondary current is the larger. Low-resistance thick wire keeps the copper loss I²R small. The secondary voltage is the lower, and it cannot carry more power than the primary supplies — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In an ideal transformer, the secondary current is larger than the primary current whenever the secondary has more turns than the primary.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Is/Ip = Np/Ns, so a secondary with more turns (step-up) carries the smaller current; the power VI is the same on both sides.

questions.stem_md: Match each energy loss in a transformer in Column A with the design feature in Column B that keeps it small.

options.text_md: Copper (I²R) loss
Eddy-current loss
Hysteresis loss
Flux leakage

match_right.text_md: A core built from thin sheets insulated by varnish
The secondary wound over the primary on a shared core
Windings of thick, low-resistance copper wire
A core of soft iron or silicon steel, easily magnetised and demagnetised

questions.solution_md: Copper loss → thick wire (1 → r); eddy-current loss → laminated core (2 → p); hysteresis loss → soft magnetic core material (3 → s); flux leakage → windings one over the other (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: A transmission line of total resistance 8.0 Ω carries 6.6 MW at 66 kV. Find the power wasted as heat in the line, in kW.
questions.solution_md: $I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{6.6 \times 10^{6}}{66 \times 10^{3}} = 100$ A; loss $= I^2R = 100^2 \times 8.0 = 80000$ W, i.e. $\dfrac{80000}{10^{3}} = 80$ kW (about 1.2% of the power).

questions.stem_md: A state transmission company raises the voltage of a line from 132 kV to 400 kV, sending the same power over the same conductors. The power wasted as heat in the line falls by a factor of about
questions.solution_md: Loss $= \dfrac{P^2R}{V^2} \propto \dfrac{1}{V^2}$: $\left(\dfrac{400}{132}\right)^2 \approx 9.2$, so the loss falls about nine times; 3 is only the factor by which the current falls — option (a).

questions.stem_md: To save the cost of transformers, a panchayat proposes taking electricity 15 km from a substation to a village at 230 V. Evaluate this proposal.

answer.model_answer_md: **Unwise.** At 230 V the current P/V would be very **large**, so the heating loss I²R and the voltage drop IR along 15 km of line would be **huge**. Stepping up the voltage cuts the current, and the loss falls as **1/V²**; a transformer near the village then gives a safe 230 V.

questions.solution_md: Low V means large I, so large I²R loss.

marking_scheme.step: Large current at low voltage gives a large I²R loss (and voltage drop)
High-voltage transmission with step-down near users is better

questions.stem_md: On what principle does a transformer work? For an ideal transformer, with no flux leakage and no energy loss, obtain the relations between the voltages, the currents and the numbers of turns of its two windings.

answer.model_answer_md:
A transformer works on **mutual induction**: the alternating current in the primary sets up an alternating flux in the core, which links the secondary and induces an emf in it.
With no flux leakage, every turn of both windings carries the same flux Φ, so $\varepsilon_p = -N_p\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$ and $\varepsilon_s = -N_s\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$. Taking $V_p \approx \varepsilon_p$ and $V_s \approx \varepsilon_s$, $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$.
With no energy loss, $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$, so $\dfrac{I_p}{I_s} = \dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$.

questions.solution_md: Same dΦ/dt per turn; power in = power out.

marking_scheme.step: Principle: mutual induction with alternating flux
Vs/Vp = Ns/Np from the same dΦ/dt per turn

questions.stem_md: (a) State Faraday’s laws of electromagnetic induction and Lenz’s law. [1] (b) A flat circular coil of 80 turns, radius 5.0 cm and resistance 4.0 Ω lies in the plane of the page, in a uniform field of 0.30 T pointing into the page. The field falls steadily to zero in 0.20 s. Find (i) the induced emf, (ii) the current, (iii) the charge that flows, (iv) the heat produced in the coil. [3] (c) State, with a reason, whether the induced current flows clockwise or anticlockwise as seen from the front. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An emf is induced in a circuit whenever the flux linked with it changes; its size equals the rate of change of flux linkage, $\varepsilon = -N\,d\Phi/dt$. Lenz’s law: the induced current opposes the change that produces it.

(b)(i) $\Delta\Phi = B\pi r^2 = 0.30 \times \pi \times (0.050)^2 \approx 2.36 \times 10^{-3}$ Wb, so $\varepsilon = \dfrac{80 \times 2.36 \times 10^{-3}}{0.20} \approx 0.942$ V.
(ii) $I = \dfrac{0.942}{4.0} \approx 0.236$ A.
(iii) $q = It \approx 0.236 \times 0.20 \approx 0.0471$ C.
(iv) $H = I^2Rt \approx 0.236^2 \times 4.0 \times 0.20 \approx 0.0444$ J.

(c) The inward flux is decreasing, so the induced current sets up an inward field to oppose the decrease: by the right-hand rule the current flows **clockwise** as seen from the front.

questions.solution_md: Faraday and Lenz; ε = NΔΦ/Δt; I, q = It, H = I²Rt; clockwise.

questions.stem_md: (a) A conducting bar of length l slides with speed v along two parallel rails joined by a resistor R, in a uniform magnetic field B perpendicular to the plane of the rails. Using Faraday’s law, derive the emf induced in the bar. [2] (b) Show that the power needed to keep the bar moving at a steady speed is (Blv)²/R, and explain how this agrees with conservation of energy. [1] (c) A bar 30 cm long, starting from rest on smooth horizontal rails joined by a 0.50 Ω resistor in a vertical field of 0.50 T, is pulled by a constant horizontal force of 0.36 N. Explain why it reaches a steady speed, and find that speed and the current at that speed. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Let the bar be at distance $x$ from the resistor. The circuit encloses area $lx$, so $\Phi = Blx$. As the bar moves, $\varepsilon = \dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = Bl\dfrac{dx}{dt} = Blv$ in size, its direction given by Lenz’s law.

(b) $I = \dfrac{Blv}{R}$, and the field exerts $F = BIl = \dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$ on the bar, opposing its motion. At steady speed the applied force equals this, so the power is $P = Fv = \dfrac{(Blv)^2}{R} = I^2R$: the mechanical work done becomes heat in the circuit, and no energy is created.

(c) The magnetic drag $\dfrac{B^2l^2v}{R}$ grows with speed until it equals the pull, after which the net force is zero. Then $v = \dfrac{FR}{B^2l^2} = \dfrac{0.36 \times 0.50}{0.50^2 \times 0.30^2} = 8.0$ m s$^{-1}$; $\varepsilon = 0.50 \times 0.30 \times 8.0 = 1.2$ V and $I = \dfrac{1.2}{0.50} = 2.4$ A (power $0.36 \times 8.0 = 2.88$ W).

questions.solution_md: Φ = Blx; F = B²l²v/R; steady when F equals the pull.

marking_scheme.step: Drag grows with v until it balances the pull

questions.stem_md: (a) Define self-inductance and derive an expression for the self-inductance of a long air-cored solenoid of N turns, length l and cross-sectional area A. [2] (b) A solenoid 50 cm long has 1000 turns of radius 2.0 cm. A small coil of 50 turns and radius 1.0 cm is placed coaxially at its centre. Find (i) the self-inductance of the solenoid, (ii) the mutual inductance of the pair, (iii) the emf induced in the small coil when a current of 2.0 A in the solenoid is switched off steadily in 4.0 ms. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Self-inductance L is the flux linkage of a coil per unit current through it, $N\Phi = LI$ (so $\varepsilon = -L\,dI/dt$). Inside the solenoid $B = \dfrac{\mu_0NI}{l}$; each turn links $BA$, so $N\Phi = \dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l}I$ and $L = \dfrac{\mu_0N^2A}{l}$.

(b)(i) $L = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1000^2 \times \pi \times (0.020)^2}{0.50} \approx 3.16 \times 10^{-3}$ H.
(ii) The solenoid’s field $\mu_0\dfrac{N}{l}I$ passes through each small turn of area $\pi r^2$: $M = \mu_0\dfrac{N}{l}N_2\pi r^2 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2000 \times 50 \times \pi \times (0.010)^2 \approx 3.95 \times 10^{-5}$ H.
(iii) $\dfrac{dI}{dt} = \dfrac{2.0}{4.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 500$ A s$^{-1}$, so $|\varepsilon| = 3.95 \times 10^{-5} \times 500 \approx 0.0197$ V (about 20 mV).

questions.solution_md: L = μ₀N²A/l; M from the solenoid field through the small coil.

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe, with a labelled diagram described in words, the construction of a transformer and explain how it works. [2] (b) Why does a transformer not work on a steady DC supply? [1] (c) A step-down transformer with 1150 primary turns gives 24 V from 230 V mains and supplies 5.0 A to a load. Its efficiency is 92%. Find the number of secondary turns, the output power and the primary current. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Two insulated copper windings, the primary ($N_p$ turns, joined to the AC supply) and the secondary ($N_s$ turns, joined to the load), are wound on a closed, laminated soft-iron core, usually one over the other. The alternating primary current sets up an alternating flux in the core; this same flux links the secondary and induces in it an alternating emf (mutual induction), with $V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p$ for an ideal transformer.

(b) A steady current produces a steady flux; with no change of flux, no emf is induced in the secondary.

(c) $N_s = N_p\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = 1150 \times \dfrac{24}{230} = 120$ turns. Output $= 24 \times 5.0 = 120$ W. Input $= \dfrac{120}{0.92} \approx 130.4$ W, so $I_p \approx \dfrac{130.4}{230} \approx 0.567$ A.

Working: alternating flux links the secondary (mutual induction)
DC: steady flux, no induced emf

questions.stem_md: A small hydroelectric station in the hills generates 1.2 MW at 6.0 kV. The power is sent to a town along a line of total resistance 12 Ω. (a) Show that, for a given power, the heating loss in a line is inversely proportional to the square of the transmission voltage. [1] (b) Find the current in the line and the power lost if the power is sent at 6.0 kV. [1] (c) An ideal transformer at the station raises the voltage to 60 kV. Find its turns ratio, the new current and the power lost, and the percentage of the generated power that reaches the town in each case. [2] (d) Why is the voltage stepped down again before the power reaches homes? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $I = \dfrac{P}{V}$, so the loss is $I^2R = \dfrac{P^2R}{V^2} \propto \dfrac{1}{V^2}$.

(b) $I = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{6}}{6.0 \times 10^{3}} = 200$ A; loss $= 200^2 \times 12 = 4.8 \times 10^{5}$ W (480 kW).

(c) $N_s : N_p = 60 : 6.0 = 10 : 1$. $I = \dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{6}}{60 \times 10^{3}} = 20$ A; loss $= 20^2 \times 12 = 4800$ W (4.8 kW). Delivered: at 6.0 kV, $1.2 - 0.48 = 0.72$ MW, i.e. 60%; at 60 kV, $1.2 - 0.0048 = 1.1952$ MW, i.e. 99.6%.

(d) Very high voltages are dangerous and need heavy insulation; step-down transformers near the users bring it to a safe 230 V.

questions.solution_md: Loss P²R/V²; I = P/V; ten times the voltage, one hundredth the loss.
